text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementNeuroscienceThe Speech Patterns of PsychosesExploring how people talk in the throes of mental health crises with McGill psychiatrist Lena PalaniyappanKFBy Kristen French1:00 PM CST on November 18, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleIn his 1955 book The Psychoses, French psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan famously argued that someone in the throes of psychosis often feels “possessed by language.” Lacan’s argument stemmed in part from an analysis of the memoirs of Daniel Paul Schreber, a 19th century German judge, who was institutionalized for close to a decade following a mental breakdown and who suffered florid hallucinations and delusions.Powered By 10 ShareNextStayLacan and Schreber both documented in vivid detail the moment in psychosis when one’s sentences become unmoored from reality. What often fills these interruptions, Lacan noticed, are wild linguistic inventions: rigid repetitive chants and neologisms with private and obscure meanings. Schreber himself coined terms such as “soul murder,“ or “miracled-up“ to describe his precarious reality. Today, clinical assessments of people with psychosis often use phrases such as “word salad,“ or “clang associations“ to describe their somersaulting patterns of speech.Read more: “The Faulty Weathermen of the Mind”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
